headings.title: Introduction to the Immune System and Its Functions
headings.content:
The human body exists in a constant state of exposure to pathogens, toxins, and abnormal cells. The immune system is the complex network of cells, tissues, and organs designed to defend the host against these microscopic invaders. Its primary mission is discrimination between self and non-self, ensuring that healthy host tissues are spared while foreign entities are neutralized. Beyond defense, the immune system plays a vital role in tissue repair, surveillance against malignant transformation, and the removal of cellular debris.

Failure of this system leads to distinct clinical extremes. When immune mechanisms are underactive, opportunistic infections thrive, a reality frequently observed in advanced HIV/AIDS or severe malnutrition. Conversely, when the system loses its ability to recognize self, it attacks native tissue, resulting in autoimmune conditions like systemic lupus erythematosus. Understanding this baseline equilibrium helps clinicians anticipate why a breakdown in immune surveillance manifests either as recurrent infections or chronic inflammatory destruction.

headings.title: Innate versus Adaptive Immunity
headings.content:
Immunity operates through two deeply integrated branches: innate and adaptive defenses. 

- **Innate Immunity**: The rapid, non-specific response present from birth. Physical barriers like the skin and mucous membranes, chemical barriers such as stomach acid, and cellular components like phagocytes act within minutes to hours of pathogen entry. It lacks immunological memory, meaning subsequent exposures elicit the exact same magnitude of response.
- **Adaptive Immunity**: The slower, highly specific system that develops after exposure to an antigen. Driven by T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes, it targets precise molecular signatures. Its hallmark feature is memory; upon re-exposure, the adaptive response is vastly accelerated and robust, forming the biological basis of successful vaccination.

headings.title: Cells and Organs of the Immune System
headings.content:
Immune cells and organs are distributed strategically throughout the body to intercept pathogens wherever they attempt entry.

| Organ/Cell Type | Primary Location | Core Function |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Bone Marrow** | Central skeletal bones | Site of hematopoiesis and B-cell maturation |
| **Thymus** | Superior mediastinum | Site of T-cell maturation and selection |
| **Lymph Nodes** | Throughout lymphatic vessels | Filter lymph and mount localized immune responses |
| **Neutrophils** | Circulating blood | Rapidly phagocytize bacteria during acute infection |
| **Macrophage** | Tissues throughout the body | Phagocytosis and antigen presentation |

headings.title: Antigens, Antibodies, and the Immune Response
headings.content:
An antigen is any substance capable of triggering an immune response, usually consisting of proteins or polysaccharides on the surface of pathogens. When a B-lymphocyte encounters its matching antigen, it differentiates into a plasma cell that secretes specialized proteins called antibodies, or immunoglobulins.

Antibodies neutralize threats through multiple pathways: they coat pathogens to mark them for phagocytosis, neutralize circulating toxins, and activate the complement cascade to lyse bacterial walls. Among the five classes of antibodies, **IgG** is the most abundant in serum and provides long-term immunity, while **IgE** mediates allergic reactions and parasite defense, and **IgA** protects mucosal surfaces found in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts.

headings.title: Inflammation and the Immune Response
headings.content:
Inflammation is a localized vascular and cellular response designed to isolate injury, destroy infectious agents, and prepare tissue for healing. The classic clinical manifestations—rubor (redness), calor (heat), tumor (swelling), dolor (pain), and functio laesa (loss of function)—stem from chemical mediators like histamine, prostaglandins, and cytokines released by damaged cells and mast cells.

These substances cause local vasodilation, increasing blood flow and capillary permeability. This vascular shift allows plasma proteins and white blood cells to leak into the interstitial space, creating edema and pressure on nerve endings. While acute inflammation is protective, chronic or uncontrolled inflammation causes extensive tissue destruction, as seen in rheumatoid arthritis or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

headings.title: Immunizations and Vaccination Principles
headings.content:
Vaccination is one of the most effective public health interventions for preventing infectious disease. Vaccines introduce harmless antigens—such as killed pathogens, weakened live organisms, or purified protein subunits—to safely stimulate the adaptive immune system without causing active disease.

This primary exposure generates clonal expansion of B and T cells and establishes immunological memory. If the individual encounters the live wild-type pathogen later, memory cells mount an immediate, high-titer antibody response that clears the infection before clinical symptoms develop. Herd immunity occurs when a large proportion of a community becomes immune, indirectly protecting vulnerable individuals who cannot be vaccinated, such as infants or the severely immunocompromised.

headings.title: Common Immune Disorders and Hypersensitivity Reactions
headings.content:
Immune dysfunction frequently manifests as overactivity or inappropriate targeting of host tissues. Hypersensitivity reactions are categorized into four classic types (Gell and Coombs classification):

1. **Type I (Immediate)**: IgE-mediated reactions, such as anaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis, and asthma, occurring rapidly after antigen exposure.
2. **Type II (Cytotoxic)**: IgG or IgM antibodies bind to cell surface antigens, triggering cell lysis, as seen in blood transfusion mismatch reactions.
3. **Type III (Immune Complex)**: Circulating antigen-antibody complexes deposit in tissue blood vessels, causing local inflammation and tissue damage, as in systemic lupus erythematosus.
4. **Type IV (Delayed-type)**: Cell-mediated reactions driven by T-lymphocytes rather than antibodies, taking 48 to 72 hours to develop, such as the tuberculin skin test or contact dermatitis from poison ivy.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Care of Immunocompromised Patients
headings.content:
Caring for immunocompromised patients—whether due to chemotherapy, immunosuppressant drugs, or viral infections—requires rigorous clinical vigilance. Because these patients lack adequate inflammatory or cellular responses, classic signs of infection like pus formation or high fever may be absent or muted. Often, a subtle change in mental status, mild tachypnea, or low-grade temperature is the only indicator of life-threatening sepsis.

Nursing care centers on protective isolation protocols, strict aseptic technique, and meticulous skin and mucous membrane assessments. Clinicians must educate patients and visitors on hand hygiene, dietary restrictions regarding unpasteurized foods or fresh produce in high-risk phases, and prompt reporting of any constitutional symptoms. Vigilance prevents preventable exposures in hospital and community settings.
